verses.text: Judah and Benjamin’s enemies heard that the people who’d come back from exile were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel.
They went to Zerubbabel and the family heads and said, “Let us build with you. We seek your God just like you do. We’ve been sacrificing to him since Esar Haddon, king of Assyria, brought us here.”

But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of Israel’s family heads told them, “You have no part with us in building a house for our God. We’ll build it ourselves, together, for the LORD, the God of Israel, just as King Cyrus of Persia told us to.”
Then the people of the land set out to discourage the people of Judah and make it hard for them to build.
They hired advisers to work against them and wreck their plans throughout the reign of King Cyrus of Persia, right up to the reign of King Darius of Persia.
At the start of Ahasuerus’s reign, they wrote an accusation against the people of Judah and Jerusalem.
In Artaxerxes’s time, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of their companions wrote to King Artaxerxes of Persia. The letter was written in Syrian script and sent in the Syrian language.
Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes making a case against Jerusalem. Here’s how it went.
It came from Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions: the Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites, Archevites, Babylonians, Shushanchites, Dehaites, and Elamites,
and the other peoples the great and noble Osnappar had brought over and settled in the city of Samaria and elsewhere in the country beyond the River, and so on.
Here’s a copy of the letter they sent: “To King Artaxerxes, from your servants, the people beyond the River.

The king should know that the Jews who came up from your territory have arrived here in Jerusalem. They’re rebuilding that wicked, rebellious city. They’ve finished the walls and repaired the foundations.
The king should also know that if the city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, they won’t pay tribute, customs duties, or tolls. In the end, that will hurt the kings.
Since we eat the salt of the palace and can’t just stand by while the king is dishonored, we’re sending word to let you know.

Have someone search the records of your ancestors. You’ll find in those records that this city is rebellious and has caused trouble for kings and provinces. There have been uprisings there before. That’s why the city was destroyed.
We’re telling the king that if the city is rebuilt and the walls are finished, you won’t have any territory left beyond the River.”
The king sent this reply to Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions living in Samaria and elsewhere beyond the River: “Peace.
The letter you sent us has been read to me clearly.
I ordered a search. It turned up that this city has risen up against kings in the past and that there have been rebellions and revolts there.
Powerful kings have also ruled Jerusalem and governed the whole country beyond the River. People paid them tribute, customs duties, and tolls.
Issue an order now to stop these men. The city is to stay unbuilt until I give the order.
See to it right away. Why let the damage grow and hurt the kings?”
When the copy of King Artaxerxes’s letter was read to Rehum, Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they rushed to the Jews in Jerusalem and used armed force to make them stop.
So the work on God’s house in Jerusalem came to a halt. It stayed that way until the second year of King Darius of Persia’s reign.
